Load the libraries

library(tidyverse)
library(janitor)
library(naniar)

Data

For this homework, we will use amniota data from: Myhrvold N, Baldridge E, Chan B, Sivam D, Freeman DL, Ernest SKM (2015). “An amniote life-history database to perform comparative analyses with birds, mammals, and reptiles.” Ecology, 96, 3109. doi: 10.1890/15-0846.1 (URL: https://doi.org/10.1890/15-0846.1).

amniota <- read_csv("data/amniota.csv") %>% 
  clean_names()
  1. Do some exploratory analysis of the amniota data set. Use the function(s) of your choice. Try to get an idea of how NA’s are represented in the data.
amniota %>% 
  glimpse()

  1. Make any necessary replacements in the data such that all NA’s appear as “NA”.
amniota <- amniota %>% 
  replace_with_na_all(condition = ~.x == -999)

  1. Use naniar to visualize the number of NA’s in each variable. Which variables have the most NA’s?
amniota %>% 
  gg_miss_var()

The variables with the most NA’s are subspecies (21322) and female_body_mass_at_maturity_g (21318).

  1. Calculate the number of NAs in the egg_mass_g column sorted by taxonomic class; i.e. how many NA’s are present in the egg_mass_g column in birds, mammals, and reptiles? Does this results make sense biologically? How do these results affect your interpretation of NA’s?
amniota %>%
  select(class, egg_mass_g) %>% 
  group_by(class) %>%
  miss_var_summary() %>% 
  arrange(desc(pct_miss))
## # A tibble: 3 × 4
## # Groups:   class [3]
##   class    variable   n_miss pct_miss
##   <chr>    <chr>       <int>    <num>
## 1 Mammalia egg_mass_g   4953    100  
## 2 Reptilia egg_mass_g   6040     92.0
## 3 Aves     egg_mass_g   4914     50.1

These results make sense as the Mammalia class (mammmals) do have 100% NA’s. Mammals are species that do not lay eggs, so it makes sense that there is no egg mass measured for them. These results showcase to me that NA’s don’t always mean that entries are sometimes forgotten, but sometimes that they can be used to say that a certain parameter don’t apply to certain entries.
